atlas-gb.0176: A High Fliers survey for 2016 hiring reported that recruiters expected a third of that year’s graduate positions to go to graduates who had already worked for them, and 77% of employers in the 2025 ISE survey say former interns are more work-ready. Year-long placements and first-year insight weeks feed the same schemes, but they are for undergraduates; a one-year master’s student has usually missed them.
atlas-gb.0177: Civil Service Fast Stream and public-sector schemes
atlas-gb.0178: The Fast Stream is a competition, not an exam: for the 2026 intake 69,046 first-preference applications led to 703 people recommended for appointment, a 1.0% success rate against 654 vacancies. Stages run from online tests and a recorded video interview to an online assessment centre and, on most schemes, a final selection board.
atlas-gb.0179: Nationals of the UK, the Republic of Ireland, the Commonwealth and the EU, Switzerland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Turkey can apply if they can live and work in the UK, but some security and intelligence posts need British citizenship.
atlas-gb.0181: 81% of ISE employers recruited apprentices in 2025, and employers hired 1.8 graduates for every apprentice, down from 2.3 a year earlier. 77% of apprenticeships went to school and college leavers and 16% to graduates, so this route is mainly for people who skip or interleave university, and apprenticeships at KPMG are not sponsored.
atlas-gb.0183: Start-ups, small firms and research groups often fill roles through direct approaches: not all internships and graduate roles are advertised, and many large companies do not accept speculative applications. Imperial’s careers service advises a named contact, a short personal email and a follow-up after 7 to 10 days.
atlas-gb.0184: Start-ups and small firms hire all year, often through networks and speculative approaches to a named person.
atlas-gb.0185: Experienced hire: advertised roles and lateral moves
atlas-gb.0186: With two to three years in a bank, lateral moves one tier at a time (boutique to middle market to bulge bracket) are the practitioner route in London, and openings come unpredictably so networking has to be continuous. This rests on one publisher’s accounts, not on counts.
atlas-gb.0187: Direct entry roles are advertised all year on boards such as Indeed, CV-Library, S1 Jobs and LinkedIn and often start soon after hiring.
atlas-gb.0188: Recruitment at the 100 leading graduate employers fell 24.5% between 2022 and 2025, and their targets for 2026 were 0.5% lower still. ISE members cut graduate hiring by 8% in a year while internship hiring rose 2%: firms kept the cheaper, earlier pipeline.
atlas-gb.0189: With fewer places, firms visit fewer campuses rather than widen their search.
atlas-gb.0190: London banks run campus events at a short list of universities (Oxford, Cambridge, LSE, Imperial, Warwick, then UCL, Durham, Bristol, Edinburgh and others). Applications open in July and close from October; a September arrival for a one-year master’s is already late.
atlas-gb.0191: The strongest master’s feeders are LSE, LBS, Imperial, Oxford and Cambridge; LBS’s Masters in Financial Analysis placed 92% within three months, two-thirds of them in the UK.
atlas-gb.0192: The Big Four take the largest graduate intakes in the country, but they shrank: about 6,500 in 2023 against 5,400 in 2024. Deloitte started 1,353 in September 2026, 44% of them outside London, so applying for Leeds, Manchester or Birmingham is a real lever.
atlas-gb.0193: Schemes fill in order of arrival and screen on grades (often a 2:1, and A-levels at EY) and online tests, not on the university’s name.
atlas-gb.0194: Consultancies open applications from October to December and hold final rounds from November to February, with case interviews.
atlas-gb.0195: Consumer-goods firms hire through rotational schemes open to any degree: Unilever’s Future Leaders Programme pays £35,000 and L’Oréal takes up to 40 marketing trainees a year in London. Both cap the time since graduating at about two years, and a failed P&G test means a twelve-month wait.
atlas-gb.0196: Industrial groups run graduate programmes with short September windows; Airbus’s UK programme does not sponsor visas.
atlas-gb.0197: The Civil Service Fast Stream is the main graduate route into government, with its own annual application window and assessment centre.
atlas-gb.0198: London is Europe’s largest tech market, but graduate hiring in UK tech fell 46% in a year. The median advertised graduate software engineer salary was £32,500, with London roles from about £40,000.
atlas-gb.0199: Big tech and fintech graduate programmes screen on hard skills: Revolut’s asks for at least a 2:1 in a STEM subject and working SQL, Python or R even for strategy roles. In one analysis of staff at Amazon, Apple, Google and Microsoft, Cambridge was the most common British university and the Open University, mostly part-time learners, the third.
atlas-gb.0200: Research roles at London’s AI labs and trading firms want a PhD or at least an MSc plus publications; IMC’s graduate machine-learning researcher needs an MSc, PhD preferred. Master’s graduates enter through data-science, analytics and applied engineering roles instead.
atlas-gb.0201: Quant desks recruit from mathematics and computing at Cambridge (Part III), Oxford and Imperial, and decide on coding and maths tests.
atlas-gb.0202: The government’s CyberFirst bursary pays students and gives summer placements leading to jobs at the NCSC, GCHQ and partner firms, but it is for British citizens only. In industry, most people start as security-operations (SOC) analysts.
atlas-gb.0203: Target universities matter for banks, top consultancies and Magic Circle law; most other employers screen on grades (often a 2:1) and tests, and many use contextual recruitment that credits strong results from a weaker school.
atlas-gb.0204: Autumn campus presentations, careers fairs and society events at target universities; employer insight days; case competitions with industry judges.
atlas-gb.0205: Autumn term is the peak: employers post and close most graduate vacancies then, some now advertise from July, and large schemes fill in order of arrival. Outside the peak, small employers, unfilled vacancies and direct roles are open all year.
atlas-gb.0206: Schemes screen on the class of the first degree, not on a master’s: the Fast Stream asks for a 2:2 or better in any subject on most schemes, and most employers screen on grades (often a 2:1). Research roles in AI are the exception and ask for an MSc or PhD.
atlas-gb.0207: Employers take foreign degrees as awarded: KPMG tells applicants to list overseas qualifications exactly as awarded, without UK equivalents. UK ENIC, run by Ecctis for the government, issues Statements of Comparability for those who need one, and regulated professions such as law, medicine, teaching and architecture have their own recognition bodies.
atlas-gb.0208: Target universities matter for banks, top consultancies and Magic Circle law; most other employers screen on grades and tests, and EY UK uses Rare’s contextual system to read applications against socio-economic background.
atlas-gb.0209: Apprenticeships are widespread but mostly for school leavers: 81% of ISE employers recruited apprentices in 2025, 77% of apprenticeships went to school and college leavers and 16% to graduates. There is no dual-study tradition like Germany’s.
atlas-gb.0210: The Fast Stream alone had 654 vacancies in the 2026 intake and 78,407 registrations. A recent ISE conference noted that the graduate downturn is concentrated in areas hit by public-sector cuts, such as education and local and central government.
atlas-gb.0211: Only licensed sponsors can sponsor, and large firms ration it: KPMG sponsors only London Audit, Tax, Consulting and Technology programmes and all Consulting Actuarial, and says the position may change at short notice; Airbus’s UK programme does not sponsor. See Visas for the rules.
atlas-gb.0212: Leave off the photo and date of birth: Prospects says you need a photo only for acting or modelling and that date of birth is irrelevant. Two pages for most graduate CVs, one page for finance and consulting, with grades shown.
atlas-gb.0213: Two A4 pages is the standard maximum for a graduate CV, and one page if the employer asks for it; a page and a half looks worse than one full page. Finance and consulting banks expect one page.
atlas-gb.0214: Many scheme forms replace the cover letter with application questions, or skip them altogether in a strength-based process; send a letter when it is asked for or when it explains a gap or a missed grade requirement.
atlas-gb.0215: Leave referees off the CV unless told otherwise, and ask your referees first. Offers are normally conditional on references and right-to-work checks.
atlas-gb.0216: You type your grades into the form and the employer checks them against transcripts or certificates later. KPMG asks for overseas qualifications as awarded and, for student-visa holders, a letter from your institution with your course completion date.
atlas-gb.0217: Scheme salaries are published, so the application does not ask for an expectation: the Fast Stream starts at £31,186 and Unilever’s Future Leaders Programme pays £35,000.
atlas-gb.0218: Employers must check the right to work before employment starts, and large firms add reference and qualification checks to the offer.
atlas-gb.0219: Online applications are the main channel for schemes; a referral gets the CV read but does not pass the tests. Smaller employers and research groups also take speculative approaches to a named person.
